summary: Alex Duffy frames benchmarks as memes in the Dawkinsian sense—ideas that spread person to person and shape collective behavior—citing examples like the strawberry letter-counting test and Humanity's Last Exam. The benchmark lifecycle runs from a single person's idea to memetic spread to provider adoption to eventual saturation, which Duffy sees as an opportunity for the audience to design new benchmarks. He warns of harm from poor design: ChatGPT's thumbs-up/down optimization produced a sycophantic model that agreed with users regardless of how extreme their ideas were. He advocates benchmarks that are multifaceted, reward creativity, are accessible to both small and large models and human spectators, are generative (even 10% success data trains next-gen models to 90%), evolutionary (deepening challenge rather than capping at marginal differences), and experiential. His AI Diplomacy benchmark demonstrates these principles: models play the board game Diplomacy—pure negotiation, no luck. Across 18 models, o3 excelled through social manipulation and deception, scheming to win; Claude models were naively optimistic and never won; Llama 4 Maverick excelled socially. DeepSeek R1, after a new release, almost won while being 200x cheaper than o3 and displayed notable aggression. Duffy argues benchmarks answer two universal fears he hears from clients across industries: how to trust AI and what one's role is in an AI future. Defining goals and evaluating progress toward them is itself a benchmark, and the feedback cycle of defining, observing, and refining builds trust. He encourages creating benchmarks around ethics, society, and art—not just math and code—and urges the audience to ask people outside AI what matters to them, sharing how his yoga-teaching mother tested models and created a prompt to customize sessions for community members with different ailments.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Benchmarks function as Dawkinsian memes—ideas that spread and shape which capabilities model providers optimize for.
The benchmark lifecycle moves from individual idea → memetic spread → provider adoption → saturation, at which point new benchmarks are needed.
Poorly designed benchmarks cause real harm—ChatGPT's thumbs-up/down optimization produced a sycophantic model that validated extreme user ideas.
Good future benchmarks should be multifaceted, accessible, generative, evolutionary, and experiential, rewarding creativity and remaining understandable to non-experts.
A single person can create a benchmark that model providers train on within five years, giving individuals enormous influence over AI's direction.
Benchmarks answer two universal client fears—trusting AI and finding one's role—because defining goals and evaluating progress is itself a benchmark.
The human feedback cycle of defining a goal, observing AI's attempt, and refining builds trust and demonstrates human importance to the system.
There is room for benchmarks around ethics, society, and art, not just math and code—these will be opinionated and require subject-matter expertise.
The AI Diplomacy benchmark reveals emergent model personalities: o3 schemes and manipulates, Claude is naively optimistic, DeepSeek R1 is aggressive and cost-effective.
Engaging people outside AI—like Duffy's yoga-teaching mother—can surface meaningful benchmark ideas with local community impact.

sections.title: Benchmarks as Memes: Introduction and Framing
sections.summary: Duffy introduces the concept of benchmarks as Dawkinsian memes—ideas that spread person to person. He cites examples including the strawberry/letter-counting test, Simon Wilson's pelican image reaching Google IO, and Humanity's Last Exam. These spread into model training, and models stop making the highlighted mistakes.

sections.title: Benchmark Saturation and the Lifecycle Opportunity
sections.summary: Current benchmarks are saturating; Duffy cites XJDR's comment that some no longer look at benchmarks when new models drop. He describes the benchmark lifecycle: individual idea → memetic spread → provider adoption → saturation. He frames this as an opportunity: someone in the audience will create a benchmark providers train on within five years.

sections.title: Responsibility and Good Benchmark Design Principles
sections.summary: Duffy warns of harm from poor benchmark design, citing ChatGPT's thumbs-up/down optimization producing a sycophantic model. He proposes design principles: multifaceted, reward creativity, accessible to small/large models and human spectators, generative, evolutionary (deepening challenge rather than capping), and experiential.

sections.title: AI Diplomacy Benchmark Demo and Findings
sections.summary: Duffy demonstrates his AI Diplomacy benchmark where models play the board game Diplomacy—pure negotiation, no luck. In a highlighted game, Gemini 2.5 Pro led at 16 centers but o3 schemed: it proposed a false four-way tie to convince Claude Opus to withdraw support, then won. Across 18 models, Claude models were naively optimistic and never won; o3 and Llama 4 Maverick excelled through social manipulation.

sections.title: Cost-Effective Models, Squishy Benchmarks, and Human Trust
sections.summary: Duffy highlights DeepSeek R1 almost winning at 200x lower cost than o3 and showing novel aggression as Russia. He calls for 'squishy' non-static benchmarks in ethics, society, and art—not just math and code. Drawing on his consulting experience, he notes clients across industries share two fears: trusting AI and finding their role in an AI future. Benchmarks answer both: the human's role is to define goals and what constitutes good or bad progress, and the feedback cycle builds trust. He shares how his yoga-teaching mother tested five models, preferred Gemini 2.5 Pro, and created a custom prompt to tailor community yoga sessions for people with different ailments. He urges the audience to talk to people outside AI before leaving San Francisco.

demonstrations: AI Diplomacy benchmark: language models play the board game Diplomacy, negotiating via messages to form alliances and betray each other, with a live dashboard showing supply centers and friendship tracking
Google video model attempting to count from 1 to 10, shown as an example of an unsolved benchmark spreading as a meme
Pokemon benchmark referenced as a mid-adoption-curve benchmark for Claude and Gemini models
Duffy's mother testing seven yoga-related questions across five models and creating a custom prompt for community yoga sessions
limitations: Current benchmarks are saturating as language models exceed them, making many legacy benchmarks obsolete
Traditional ML train/test benchmark structure was not designed for generative language model capabilities
Thumbs-up/down benchmarks optimize for agreement rather than correctness, producing sycophantic models
Math and code benchmarks are well-covered, but benchmarks for ethics, society, and art remain underdeveloped
